4388.stem:
The diagram shows the location of three places $X$, $Y$ and $C$.

$Y$ is on a bearing of $120^\circ$ and 15 km from $X$.

$C$ is 40 km from $X$ and lies due west of $Y$.

$P$ lies on the line joining $C$ and $Y$ and is due south of $X$.

\exfigure{300_q27_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram with X, Y, C, P
solution sketch: bearings diagram with angles marked

parts.latex: Find the distance from $X$ to $P$.
What is the bearing of $C$ from $X$, to the nearest degree?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{300_q27_s1}

Due south of $X$ is a straight line, so $\angle PXY$ is supplementary to the bearing $120^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle PXY &= 180^\circ-120^\circ\\ &= 60^\circ\end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $PXY$, $XP$ is adjacent to $\angle PXY$.
$$\begin{aligned}XP &= 15\times\cos 60^\circ\\ &= 7.5 \text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies an angle in triangle $PXY$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{300_q27_s1}

In right-angled triangle $CXP$, let $\theta = \angle CXP$, with $XP = 7.5$ km and $XC = 40$ km.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\theta &= \dfrac{7.5}{40}\\ \theta &\approx 79^\circ 12'\end{aligned}$$
$C$ is south-west of $X$, so the bearing is measured past south.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Bearing of } C &= 180^\circ+79^\circ 12'\\ &= 259^\circ 12'\\ &\approx 259^\circ\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } C \text{ from } X \text{ is } 259^\circ$$
criteria: Calculates one of the acute angles in triangle $CXP$, or equivalent merit

300_q27_1.notes: Bearings diagram copied from the crop (NOT TO SCALE): N and E axes through X with bold N/E labels and filled arrowheads, and triangle C-X-Y with XP due south and a right-angle mark at P. The 120 degree bearing arc is a true circle centred on X: it starts on the north line and its arrowhead ends exactly on XY. Labels 40 km, 15 km, NOT TO SCALE are in the crop's positions. Rules 1, 4, 12, 14, 22.

300_q27_s1.notes: Same bearings diagram as the question, plus the solution's theta (angle CXP) and 60 degree (angle PXY) labels beside XP, as in the solution crop. The 120 degree arc is centred on X and ends on XY. Labels are clear of all lines. The remaining colour is small label and glyph offsets and the NOT TO SCALE position. Rules 1, 11, 12, 18, 22.

figures.cap: rectangle with circular arc PQ on side AB

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a shape $APQBCD$. The shape consists of a rectangle $ABCD$ with an arc $PQ$ on side $AB$ and with side lengths $BC = 3.6$ m and $CD = 8.0$ m.

The arc $PQ$ is an arc of a circle with centre $O$ and radius 2.1 m and $\angle POQ = 110^\circ$.

\exfigure{300_q33_1}

What is the perimeter of the shape $APQBCD$? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter includes the arc $PQ$, but not the chord $PQ$. The chord is needed to find $AP+QB$.

Arc length, using $\ell = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\times 2\pi r$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Arc } PQ &= \dfrac{110}{360}\times 2\times\pi\times 2.1\\ &\approx 4.0317\end{aligned}$$
Chord $PQ$, by the cosine rule in triangle $POQ$:
$$\begin{aligned}PQ &= \sqrt{2.1^2+2.1^2-2\times 2.1\times 2.1\cos 110^\circ}\\ &\approx 3.4404\end{aligned}$$
The sides $AP$ and $QB$ together are $8.0-3.4404$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Perimeter} &= 3.6\times 2+8.0+(8.0-3.4404)+4.0317\\ &\approx 23.79\\ &\approx 23.8 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the arc length AND the length of line segment $PQ$, or equivalent merit
Calculates the arc length OR the length of line segment $PQ$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to calculate the perimeter of the shape by adding some appropriate portions, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added a short explanation of why the chord is needed; source maths unchanged.

PQ, OP and OQ are dashed in the house aux style and O is a dot. '2.1 m' is rotated along OQ as in the crop. NOT TO SCALE is kept and the layout follows the crop (rule 1). Rules 1, 3, 6a, 19.

parts.latex: Which true bearing is the same as $\text{S}48^\circ\text{W}$?

solutions.latex:
A bearing of $\text{S}48^\circ\text{W}$ is measured $48^\circ$ from south towards west.

South is $180^\circ$ true, and west is $270^\circ$ true, so turning towards west adds to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{True bearing} &= 180^\circ + 48^\circ \\ &= 228^\circ \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

meta.self_check: S48W lies in the south-west quadrant: 180+48=228.

figures.cap: triangular prism dam

parts.latex:
A dam is in the shape of a triangular prism which is 50 m long, as shown.

Both ends of the dam, $ABC$ and $DEF$, are isosceles triangles with equal sides of length 25 metres. The included angles $BAC$ and $EDF$ are each $150^\circ$.

\exfigure{271_q28_1}

Calculate the number of litres of water the dam will hold when full.

solutions.latex:
The cross-section is a triangle with two sides of 25 m and included angle $150^\circ$, so use the area formula $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 25\times 25\times \sin 150^\circ \\ &= 156.25 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
The volume is the cross-sectional area times the length.
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 156.25 \times 50 \\ &= 7812.5 \text{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1000 \text{ L}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Litres} &= 7812.5 \times 1000 \\ &= 7\,812\,500 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the dam holds } 7\,812\,500 \text{ L}$$
criteria: Finds the volume of the dam in $\text{m}^3$, or equivalent merit
Finds the area of the base triangle, or equivalent merit
Attempts to find the area of the base, or equivalent merit

The 150° arc is centred at A and ends on AB and AC, with the label haloed on the stipple (rule 5b). Equal-side ticks on AB and AC; 50 m, 25 m and NOT TO SCALE kept. 4432.stem:
The diagram shows an aeroplane that was flying towards an airport at $A$ on a bearing of $135^\circ\text{T}$. When it was at point $O$, 20 km away from the airport at $A$, the flight course was changed. The aeroplane landed at an airport at $B$ directly south of $O$. The distance from $O$ to $B$ is 50 km.

\exfigure{271_q33_1}

figures.cap: flight path diagram O, A, B
solution sketch: labelled flight diagram

parts.latex: Show that the distance between the airport at $A$ and the airport at $B$ is 38.5 km, correct to 1 decimal place.
Use the sine rule to find the angle $OBA$ to the nearest degree.
What is the bearing of the airport at $B$ from the airport at $A$?

criteria: Attempts to use the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule in triangle $OAB$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle OBA}{20} = \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{38.5}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\angle OBA &= \dfrac{20\sin 45^\circ}{38.5} \\ &= 0.3673\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle OBA = 22^\circ \text{ (nearest degree)}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the sine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ + 22^\circ \\ &= 202^\circ\text{T} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $\theta$, correct to the nearest degree.
Find the value of $x$, correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle, the tangent ratio uses the opposite side 8 and the adjacent side 10.
$$\tan\theta = \dfrac{8}{10}$$
$$\theta = 39^\circ \text{ (nearest degree)}$$
criteria: Uses the correct trigonometric ratio, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right-angled triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 10^2 + 8^2 \\ &= 164 \\ x &= \sqrt{164} \\ &\approx 12.8 \text{ (one decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use a relevant trigonometric ratio or attempts to use Pythagoras' theorem, or equivalent merit

4509.stem:
Mr Ali, Ms Brown and a group of students were camping at the site located at $P$. Mr Ali walked with some of the students on a bearing of $035^\circ$ for 7 km to location $A$. Ms Brown, with the rest of the students, walked on a bearing of $100^\circ$ for 9 km to location $B$.

\exfigure{36_q31_1}

figures.cap: bearings diagram P, A, B

parts.latex: Show that the angle $APB$ is $65^\circ$.
Find the distance $AB$.
Find the bearing of Ms Brown's group from Mr Ali's group. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
North lines at $P$ give the bearings measured clockwise from north.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle APB &= 100^\circ-35^\circ \\ &= 65^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Using the cosine rule in $\triangle APB$:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= 7^2+9^2-2\times 7\times 9\cos 65^\circ \\ &= 76.75\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ AB \approx 8.76 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the cosine rule to find the distance $AB$

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule in $\triangle APB$ to find $\angle PAB$:
$$\dfrac{\sin A}{9} = \dfrac{\sin 65^\circ}{8.76\ldots}$$
$$A = 68.6\ldots^\circ \approx 69^\circ$$
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is found using the angle at $A$ and the north line at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ-(69^\circ-35^\circ) \\ &= 146^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds another angle in $\triangle APB$, or equivalent merit

36_q31_1.notes: North line with a filled arrowhead and bold N. P, A and B as dots, with segment labels 7 km and 9 km placed as in the crop. The angles are copied from the crop, which is a sketch, not redrawn to the true bearings 035/100 (rule 1). Rules 1, 4, 6a.

figures.cap: regular decagon with centre O

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a regular decagon (ten-sided shape with all sides equal and all interior angles equal). The decagon has centre $O$.

\exfigure{36_q32_1}

The perimeter of the shape is 80 cm.

By considering triangle $OAB$, calculate the area of the ten-sided shape. Give your answer in square centimetres correct to one decimal place.
can_use: Area of a triangle (1/2 ab sin C)

solutions.latex:
The ten sides are equal, so
$$AB = 80\div 10 = 8 \text{ cm}$$
The ten angles at the centre are equal:
$$\angle AOB = 360^\circ\div 10 = 36^\circ$$
Triangle $OAB$ is isosceles ($OA=OB=r$), so
$$\angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ-36^\circ}{2} = 72^\circ$$
Using the sine rule in $\triangle OAB$:
$$\dfrac{r}{\sin 72^\circ} = \dfrac{8}{\sin 36^\circ}$$
$$r = 12.944\ldots$$
The area is ten times the area of $\triangle OAB$:
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 10\times\dfrac{1}{2}\times(12.944\ldots)^2\times\sin 36^\circ \\ &\approx 492.4 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates area of $\triangle AOB$, or equivalent merit

36_q32_1.notes: Regular decagon (circumradius 157 px, centre O) with side AB on top. OA and OB are dashed (aux), each with one equal-length tick at its midpoint. O is a dot with its label below. Rules 1, 3, 6a, 19.

parts.latex: What compass bearing is equivalent to a true bearing of $245^\circ$?

solutions.latex:
A true bearing of $245^\circ$ lies between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$, so it is in the south-west quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 245^\circ - 180^\circ &= 65^\circ \end{aligned}$$
So the direction is $65^\circ$ west of south, that is S$65^\circ$W, which is option C.

The side $37$ is opposite the $27^\circ$ angle and $x$ is the hypotenuse, so use sine.
$$\sin 27^\circ = \dfrac{37}{x}$$
$$x = \dfrac{37}{\sin 27^\circ}$$
This is option B.

figures.cap: Nadia 1.6 m tall, 8 m from a tree of height h with a bird at the top

solutions.latex:
The angle of depression of Nadia from the bird equals the angle of elevation of the bird from Nadia, $73^\circ$. In the right-angled triangle, the height of the bird above Nadia's eye level is $h$, and the horizontal distance is $8$ m.
$$\tan 73^\circ = \dfrac{h}{8}$$
$$h = 8\tan 73^\circ$$
Add Nadia's height.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Height of tree} &= 8\tan 73^\circ + 1.6 \\ &\approx 27.77 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

4537.stem:
A grandstand at an oval is shown in cross-section $BCDE$.

The seating, along the interval $DE$, is angled at $\alpha^\circ$ to the horizontal and begins 4 m above ground level.

From $B$, Aiden measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $51^\circ$, then walks 44 m onto the field and measures the angle of elevation of $D$ to be $28^\circ$ from point $A$.

\exfigure{722_q14_1}

figures.cap: grandstand cross-section with points A, B, C, D, E, F, angles 28° and 51°, AB = 44 m, EB = FC = 4 m

parts.latex: Show that $\angle ADB = 23^\circ$
Calculate the distance $BD$ correct to the nearest metre.
Calculate the distance $DF$ and hence find the angle of the seating, $\alpha$, to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
Since $\angle ABD$ and the $51^\circ$ elevation angle lie on a straight line, they are supplementary.
$$\angle ABD = 180^\circ - 51^\circ = 129^\circ$$
In $\triangle ABD$, the angle at $A$ is $28^\circ$. By the angle sum of a triangle:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ADB + 28^\circ + 129^\circ &= 180^\circ \\ \angle ADB &= 23^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: A solution diagram would help but the question's figure is used.

solutions.latex:
Use the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$.
$$\dfrac{BD}{\sin 28^\circ} = \dfrac{44}{\sin 23^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned} BD &= \dfrac{44\sin 28^\circ}{\sin 23^\circ} \\ &\approx 53 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the correct sine rule equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle BCD$, with $BD = 53$ and angle $51^\circ$ at $B$:
$$\sin 51^\circ = \dfrac{DC}{53}$$
$$\begin{aligned} DC &= 53\sin 51^\circ \\ &\approx 41.19 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The seating begins $4$ m above ground, so
$$DF = DC - 4 = 53\sin 51^\circ - 4$$
Also
$$\cos 51^\circ = \dfrac{BC}{53}$$
$$BC = 53\cos 51^\circ$$
The seating angle satisfies
$$\tan\alpha = \dfrac{53\sin 51^\circ - 4}{53\cos 51^\circ}$$
$$\therefore\ \alpha \approx 48^\circ$$
criteria: Finds $DF$ and sets up $\tan\alpha$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source takes tan α with opposite = DF and adjacent = BC; kept as given, and the value was not rechecked.

Labels on the shading use \halo. BCDE has the crop's fine diagonal-line shading, drawn with house shade hatch (rule 5). The low redraw score comes only from the hatch lines: the scan's hatching is much finer and reads as light grey. The 28 deg arc stays at the crop's drawn angle (26.7 deg), following rule 1. Rules used: 1, 3, 4, 5, 5b, 11, 14, 22. Checker 23 Nov fix: shaded area is plain grey, no stripes.

parts.latex:
In triangle $DEF$, $\angle EDF = 44^\circ$, $EF = 6$ cm, and $DE = 7$ cm.

Find $\angle EFD$ to the nearest degree, given that it is obtuse.

solutions.latex:
Use the sine rule in $\triangle DEF$.
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle EFD}{7} = \dfrac{\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
$$\sin\angle EFD = \dfrac{7\sin 44^\circ}{6}$$
The acute solution is $54^\circ$.
$$\angle EFD \approx 54^\circ$$
The angle is obtuse, so take the supplement.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle EFD &= 180^\circ - 54^\circ \\ &= 126^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the sine rule to find the acute angle, or equivalent merit

4539.stem:
Chris completed a radial survey of one of his paddocks, which he has labelled $ABCD$, from a point $O$ inside the paddock.

Using his measurements, he has calculated the length of three of the boundaries and the area of three of the triangular sections of the paddock.

His measurements and the results of his calculations are shown on the diagram below.

\exfigure{722_q16_1}

figures.cap: radial survey of paddock ABCD from point O with bearings, lengths and areas

parts.latex: Show that $\angle AOB = 138^\circ$.
Hence, calculate the length of the boundary $AB$ and find the perimeter of the paddock. Answer to 1 decimal place.
Calculate the area of the entire paddock. Answer to the nearest square kilometre.

solutions.latex:
The angle $\angle AOB$ is made up of $\angle AON$ and $\angle NOB$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AOB &= \angle AON + \angle NOB \\ &= 60^\circ + 78^\circ \\ &= 138^\circ \end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle AOB$, use the cosine rule with $\angle AOB = 138^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2 &= 1.4^2 + 2.2^2 - 2\times 1.4\times 2.2\cos 138^\circ \\ &= 11.377\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} AB &= 3.373\ldots \\ &\approx 3.4 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is the sum of the four boundaries.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Perimeter} &= 3.4 + 2.5 + 1.5 + 2.2 \\ &= 9.6 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ AB \approx 3.4 \text{ km and perimeter} = 9.6 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Finds the length of $AB$ and attempts the perimeter, or equivalent merit
Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Sides 2.5 and 1.5 and 2.2 read from the figure as in source.

solutions.latex:
The area of $\triangle DOC$ uses $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 1.5\times 1.7\times \sin 85^\circ \\ &= 1.2701\ldots \text{ km}^2 \\ &\approx 1.3 \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Add the four triangle areas.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of paddock} &= 4.4 + 1.0 + 1.8 + 1.2701\ldots \\ &= 8.47\ldots \text{ km}^2 \\ &\approx 8 \text{ km}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Area} \approx 8 \text{ km}^2$$
criteria: Finds the area of $\triangle DOC$, or equivalent merit

The angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so
$$\angle YXZ = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 65^\circ = 55^\circ$$
The sides $XY$ and $XZ$ enclose this angle, so use the area formula $A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 12 \times \sin 55^\circ \\ &\approx 73.7 \text{ cm}^2 \\ &\approx 74 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
A yacht race takes a triangular course. Yachts leave from $A$ and travel on a bearing of $294^\circ$ for 18 km to a buoy at $B$.

From $B$ the yachts travel due south to another buoy at $C$.

The final leg of the race is on a bearing of $030^\circ$ from $C$ back to finish at $A$.

\exfigure{15_q41_1}

What is the total length of the race, in kilometres, correct to three significant figures?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{15_q41_s2}

$$\sin 32^\circ = \dfrac{7}{d}$$

$$\begin{aligned} d &= \dfrac{7}{\sin 32^\circ} \\ &\approx 13.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Hence the answer is option D.

solutions.latex:
In right-angled $\triangle OAB$, by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} OA^2 &= 12^2 + 5^2 = 169 \\ OA &= 13 \text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
Since $AX = 7$, the radius is $13 - 7 = 6$ cm.
$$\angle AOB = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) = 22.62^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area of } \triangle OAB &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 5 = 30 \text{ cm}^2 \\ \text{Area of sector } XOY &= \dfrac{22.62}{360} \times \pi \times 6^2 = 7.106 \text{ cm}^2 \\ \text{Shaded area} &= 30 - 7.106 = 22.8938\ldots \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage} &= \dfrac{22.894}{30} \times 100\% \\ &= 76.3\% \text{ (to 1 decimal place)} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The diagram shows a block of land $ABCD$. It also shows the bearing of each of the points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, from point $O$.

\exfigure{5836_q35_1}

The distance from $O$ to $C$ is 25 km, $OA = OB$ and $\angle AOB = 45^\circ$.

The area of the shaded triangle $AOB$ is $80\text{ km}^2$.

What is the distance from $B$ to $C$, to the nearest kilometre?

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ with $OA = OB = a$:
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &= \dfrac{1}{2}a^2\sin 45^\circ \\ 160 &= a^2\sin 45^\circ \\ a^2 &= \dfrac{160}{\sin 45^\circ} \\ a &= 15.042\ldots \end{aligned}$$
Applying the cosine rule in $\triangle OBC$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 25^2 + 15.042\ldots^2 - 2 \times 25 \times 15.042\ldots \cos 152^\circ \\ &= 1515.357\ldots \\ BC &= 38.927\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC \approx 39 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule with $152^\circ$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A ship sails 8 km from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $070^\circ$. It then sails from $B$ to $C$.

Point $D$ lies on the line $CE$ and is 5 km due east of $B$, and $E$ is 8.7 km due south of $C$ and directly east of $A$.

\exfigure{5836_q37_1}

What is the true bearing of $A$ from $C$, correct to the nearest degree?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{5836_q37_s1}

In the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $AB = 8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos 20^\circ &= \dfrac{AF}{8} \\ AF &= 7.517\ldots \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$AE = 7.517\ldots + 5 \approx 12.52 \text{ km}$$

\exfigure{5836_q37_s2}

In the right-angled triangle $ACE$:
$$\angle ACE = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12.52}{8.7}\right) = 55.2^\circ$$
The bearing of $A$ from $C$ is
$$180^\circ + 55.2^\circ = 235.2^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Bearing} \approx 235^\circ$$
criteria: Attempts to find $AF$, or equivalent merit
